Procedural justice: fairness of process as distinct from fairness of outcome

claims.claim: Justice applies to individual actions, laws, public policies, and social structures, and philosophical discussion treats it as a family of concepts rather than a single rule.

Distributive justice concerns how benefits and burdens such as income, wealth, opportunities, jobs, and welfare should be distributed; principles vary in what is distributed, to whom, and on what basis.

Corrective justice is a bilateral remedial principle: when one person wrongly interferes with another's legitimate holdings, justice requires restoring the victim, for example by returning stolen property.

Retributive justice holds that those who commit serious wrongs morally deserve punishment proportionate to the gravity of the wrong, and that punishing the innocent or inflicting disproportionate punishment is unjust; desert and proportionality remain contested notions.

Procedural justice concerns the fairness of the process by which benefits and burdens are allocated, distinct from the justice of the final allocation; Rawls distinguished perfect, imperfect, and pure procedural justice.
Strict egalitarianism holds that every person should receive the same level of material goods and services, commonly justified by the moral equality of persons.

Rawls's difference principle permits social and economic inequalities only when they make the least advantaged members of society materially better off than they would be under strict equality; his overall theory is known as justice as fairness.

Nozick's entitlement theory holds that a distribution is just if everyone is entitled to their holdings through just acquisition and just transfer; justice tracks the history of holdings rather than requiring any overall pattern.
Welfare-based distributive principles, of which utilitarianism is the most famous variant, assess arrangements by their effects on welfare rather than by material equality.
Desert-based distributive principles allocate according to what people deserve through their actions, with contemporary proposals typically grounding desert in contribution, effort, or compensation.

Restorative justice is an approach to wrongdoing that focuses on repairing harm to victims, offenders, and communities, with outcomes such as restitution, community service, and victim-offender reconciliation, presented as an alternative to punishment-focused retributive justice.

Choosing among distributive principles is a contested methodological task; a survey can present the main positions and their criticisms neutrally, and describing a theory is distinct from endorsing it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What basis should determine distributive shares: equality, desert, or need?
positions: Egalitarian views treat equal shares as the default unless special claims justify more for some.
Desert-based views tie shares to contribution, effort, or costs borne.
Need-based and welfare-based criteria assess shares by needs or overall well-being.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents these as competing criteria within distributive justice and does not select one as correct.

positions: Strictly equal bundles can be inefficient: voluntary trades could make some people better off without harming anyone else (Pareto-superior allocations).
Pursuing an overall pattern such as equality can conflict with liberty and voluntary exchange, as libertarian critics of patterned theories argue.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes the tension neutrally and illustrates it with ordinary cases rather than adjudicating it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether retributive punishment is justified and what proportionality requires.
positions: Retributive justice holds that wrongdoers deserve proportionate punishment and that punishing the innocent or disproportionately is unjust.
The notions of desert, proportionality, the normative status of suffering, and the ultimate justification of punishment remain contested among philosophers.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the retributive view and flags the contestation without endorsing any position on punishment.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft treats justice as a generic 'foundational concept' and a 'label on a toolbox drawer' without identifying the distinct forms of justice.
The draft's question bank (three 3-option items) tests generic study skills rather than the content of justice.

sourceRecords.title: Justice
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 (first published 2017-06-26; substantive revision 2026-01-19). Supports the family-of-concepts framing, corrective vs distributive justice, procedural vs substantive justice including Rawls's perfect/imperfect/pure procedural justice, Nozick's historical/end-state/patterned distinction, the egalitarian default in the absence of special claims, and utilitarian approaches to justice. Reference only; all lesson prose is original synthesis.

sourceRecords.title: Distributive Justice
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 (first published 1996-09-22; substantive revision 2017-09-26). Supports the scope of distributive justice (benefits and burdens; income, wealth, opportunities, jobs), strict egalitarianism, Rawls's two principles and the difference principle, welfare-based (utilitarian) principles, desert-based principles (contribution, effort, compensation; the Lockean labor tradition), Nozick's entitlement theory (justice in acquisition and transfer), and the methodology section's point that choosing among principles is contested. Reference only; original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Retributive Justice
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 (first published 2014-06-18; substantive revision 2020-07-31). Supports the three principles of retributive justice: wrongdoers deserve proportionate punishment, giving it is intrinsically good, and punishing the innocent or inflicting disproportionate punishment is impermissible; also supports the observation that desert, proportionality, and the justification of punishment remain contested. Reference only.
